reference.source: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases / WHO guidance
clinicalPearls: A mosquito-borne phlebovirus zoonosis of sub-Saharan Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, with epizootics in livestock heralding human outbreaks, often after heavy rainfall and flooding
Humans are most often infected through direct contact with the blood or tissues of infected animals (abattoir workers, herders, veterinarians) as well as by mosquito bites
Most infections are a self-limiting influenza-like febrile illness, but a minority develop severe disease with haemorrhagic fever, hepatitis, encephalitis, or retinitis
A characteristic delayed ocular complication is macular or paramacular retinitis that can cause permanent visual loss weeks after the acute illness
The haemorrhagic form features jaundice, mucosal bleeding, and hepatic necrosis and carries a high mortality
Management is supportive; there is no licensed specific antiviral, and ribavirin has been considered in some settings for other viral haemorrhagic fevers but is not established for Rift Valley fever
Diagnosis uses RT-PCR and serology (IgM/IgG), and laboratory handling requires enhanced biosafety because of aerosol infectivity
reference.pathophysiology: Rift Valley fever virus is transmitted by infected mosquitoes and by direct contact with aerosols or fluids from viraemic animals during slaughter or handling. After entry the virus replicates widely and is markedly hepatotropic, producing hepatocellular necrosis. Severe disease reflects a combination of direct viral injury, cytokine-driven vascular dysfunction, and coagulopathy, leading to haemorrhage, hepatic failure, or central nervous system and retinal involvement. Immune-mediated inflammation contributes to the delayed retinitis and encephalitic complications.
additionalDifferentials: Other viral haemorrhagic fevers such as Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever or Ebola virus disease
Q fever and other zoonotic febrile illnesses
additionalInvestigations: RT-PCR on blood for viral RNA in the acute viraemic phase
Serology for Rift Valley fever IgM and IgG antibodies
Liver function tests to detect hepatitis and hepatic necrosis
Full blood count and coagulation studies to assess for haemorrhagic disease
Ophthalmological examination for retinitis in patients with visual symptoms
Lumbar puncture and neuroimaging when encephalitis is suspected
redFlags: Jaundice with mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding indicating the haemorrhagic form
Rapidly rising transaminases signalling fulminant hepatitis
Altered consciousness or focal neurological signs of encephalitis
reference.prognosis: The great majority recover fully from the uncomplicated febrile illness, but the haemorrhagic and encephalitic forms carry substantial mortality, and retinitis may leave permanent visual impairment.
pitfalls: Assuming a benign course when severe hepatic, haemorrhagic, or neurological disease can develop in a minority
Failing to recognise delayed retinitis presenting weeks after apparent recovery
Inadequate biosafety precautions given aerosol transmissibility in the laboratory and abattoir setting
Overlooking the animal-contact or outbreak history in endemic regions
Confusing early disease with malaria and delaying appropriate isolation and diagnostics
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
World Health Organization Rift Valley fever fact sheet and guidance
management: Supportive care as there is no licensed specific antiviral, with fluid, electrolyte and organ support for the febrile illness
Intensive management of the haemorrhagic form, correcting coagulopathy and transfusing blood products, with support for hepatic failure
Supportive neurological care and airway protection for the encephalitic form
Ophthalmological review and corticosteroid consideration for the delayed macular retinitis threatening vision
Infection prevention with barrier precautions when handling blood and body fluids, given aerosol and contact transmission
Personal protection for abattoir workers, herders and veterinarians, supported by livestock vaccination and mosquito vector control
Public-health and veterinary coordination during epizootics that herald human outbreaks
